sm: Doug Wilson answers a listener who wonders whether to encourage two daughters to attend college when he hopes they will marry and raise families. Wilson says he would like to see fewer college degrees but of higher quality, since there is a difference between getting an education and merely getting certified. He says about ninety percent of colleges are not worth considering, and parents should ask which college, how far it is from home, how rooted the daughters are, and whether there is a good worshiping community. He argues that education and motherhood are not opposed, because a mother's education shapes what her children and grandchildren receive. A liberal arts education equips a woman for many paths, including being a stay-at-home mom, though a woman without college can also be well equipped for that role.

Wilson continues that raising standards will produce a more stratified society, and he says Christians should not be embarrassed by that. He points to the Reformation's recovery of the dignity of all lawful work, from backhoe operator to attorney to preacher, and says differences in pay and standing reflect differences in ability and training. Ambition is not a moral duty, but some people are given a large vision, as Solomon was, and they need a rigorous education. To decide who should go, he suggests looking at what a student loves to read and study, and letting the process weed people out. On the idea of college as something to fall back on, he says it is a fallen world and that can be useful, but it is hazardous to think that way. He prefers telling a daughter to be fruitful while she waits.
